chapter: Running the band on the road
title: Percentage dances and the Thomasville arrest
summary: Albert explains why he guarded the door at percentage dances, and tells how in Thomasville, Georgia the police arrested the whole band and threatened to shoot him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When you were working on the percentage, you would watch the game.

Well, now there you go again. A lot of times they asked me why did I stop playing like I did. Well, for more reasons than one. That was one of them to stay on the door and watch the proceedings there and make sure that I got everything was mine. That's what happened when we were on the verge of being lynched in Thomasville, Georgia, playing a percentage dance and the school teacher had charge of the dance. And naturally I was up there checking the door with him when the policemen came in to arrest everybody, including the band and me. I took the money out of the drawer and put it in my pocket to make sure that I wasn't going to be on the losing end all the way around. But I was on the losing end because in a way when this fellow, the captain, whoever he was, arrested the whole band and arrested me and attempted to shoot me six of them in the hall. Well, they got us down to the jailhouse and I had given one of the girls in the band that used to dance. Her name was James. Her last name was James. And I had given her most of the money to hold so when we got into the jailhouse, it was a small place. They put 19 of us in one room. But a couple of the guys had gotten away and Mickey Alcorn happened to be one of them. And Kato was the bass player. And they had torn up all the instruments. The guys had just thrown chairs and everything else. They're the ones that started to fight. So this officer there, I guess he was a captain, he told me to put my money out of my pocket on the table. So I put what I had in my pocket, which a monitor made about $35 or $40. And he told me, well, that wasn't enough. I want all the money. And he said, you're over there charging those. Well, can I use the words that he used? He says, you're charging those niggers too much money over there, 75 cents a head to hear that rock music. And he said, that's too much money. And he said, I know you got more money than that. Well, I said, yes, possibly so. I said, but all I have is what I've put there. He said, well, I want all of the money. So I told the girl to put the money on the desk and she counted it out to him. Well, I said, I'd like to have a receipt for that money. He said, this is going to be a fine. And he called me a smart nigger from New York and of course, showed you how stupid he was. The license on the bus was Texas license. Well, to make a long story short, I asked him for a trial before a judge. And he said, well, I'm setting this fine where this judge is going to set it. I'm sure he's going to set it like that. And there's an entrance and an outlet to Thomasville, Georgia. I want you to use both of them. See if you've already used the entrance and I use the exit. I told him, thank you. And got in the bus. Well, my father, I was traveling with him. He was acting as a bus driver in a valley. And we stopped in a service station on the way out. We're going to Macon, Georgia for the next night. Well, we were busted. We didn't have anything. So I asked the attendant there, would he trust me with 150 gallons of gas? Because that's what the bus used. It used 75 gallons on one side, one tank and 75 on the other tank. And I said, I would like to have five gallons of gas. Oh, you say, I mean, all right. He said, oh, you the fellas were in that trouble tonight. I said, that's right. I said, but if you trust me with this, as soon as I get to Macon, mister, I'll send you your money. He said, okay. And he filled up both of the tanks and gave me five gallons of gas. Well, as soon as I got to Macon, Georgia, I went to a doctor friend of mine and was connected with the promotion of the band, Dr. Frasier. And I told him the situation, how it was, and how bad it had been. He says, well, sure, we'll send a fella the money. So we sent it to him right away. And naturally from an incident such as that in the days, then the Pittsburgh Courier took up the complaint from me and they wrote a massive story on it. And that's one of the incidents that I have always wanted to talk to you about. I don't think I have ever talked to you on this thing before. That was one of the sad parts of being a Negro band and traveling through the south and things like that after they find out that you are a Negro band.
